one_liner: Macro-free C++20 single-header/module unit-testing framework whose 2019 benchmark compiled faster than Boost.Test, GoogleTest and Catch2.
what_it_does: UT ("[Boost].UT", not an official Boost library) is a unit-testing framework written with C++20 language features instead of macros: tests are written as "name"_test = [] { ... };, assertions as expect(...), and suites as static boost::ut::suite objects, with sections, BDD/Gherkin/Spec aliases and parameterized tests through generic lambdas. It ships as one header (boost/ut.hpp) or a C++20 module (import boost.ut), and the runner, reporter and printer can be replaced through the cfg<override> variable template. The API is different from GoogleTest, Catch2 and doctest, so adopting it means rewriting tests; macros are opt-in wrappers you define yourself.
how_it_is_fast: The README's FAQ credits a few design choices: tests are assigned through a plain function pointer (operator=(void (*)())) rather than a template instantiated for every lambda type (the header comment says this 'compiles 5x faster', with no benchmark attached); type-name erasure so comparison objects such as eq<int, int> can be memoized; simplified internal versions of std::function and std::string_view; and a single header with few includes. In the benchmarked UT 1.1.0 the test files defined BOOST_UT_INTERFACE and saw only a slim interface (7 standard includes), with the runner compiled once in a BOOST_UT_IMPLEMENTATION translation unit; that split is absent from v1.1.9 onward, and v2.0.0 through v2.3.1 include 25 standard headers plus <format> and <source_location> when available.
when_to_use: C++20 code bases that want macro-free tests using std::source_location, concepts and designated-initializer configuration

Moving off Boost.Test, GoogleTest or a Catch2 v2 single header where test-code compile time hurts: on the 2019 100-file suite with STL asserts (clang9 default) UT took about 55 s against about 195 s, 130 s and 110 s (chart readings)
Many small test cases per file: 1,000 empty tests in one file compiled in about 1 s against about 2.2 s (doctest) to 7 s (Boost.Test) with clang9 default
Projects that want a test framework consumable as a C++20 module or need a custom runner/reporter (for example JUnit output) without forking the framework
when_not_to_use: Anything below C++20, or Clang 12-16 with libstdc++: issue #637 (open) reports segfaults and silently skipped tests traced to initialization-order assumptions for the cfg variable template; workarounds are a single test TU with cfg instantiated first, -stdlib=libc++, or staying on v1.1.9

Large multi-file suites where doctest is the alternative: on the same 2019 chart doctest compiled the 100-file suite about as fast as UT in default and -g modes and faster with clang9 -O3 (about 145 s vs 215 s); UT led only with gcc9 -O3 (about 230 s vs 270 s)

Expecting the published numbers to hold for current UT: they measure 1.1.0 with the interface/implementation split; the current header pulls in more than three times as many standard headers (25 against 7) and has not been re-benchmarked

Needing built-in mocking (the README points to GUnit, FakeIt or hippomocks), abort/death checks on Windows (aborts() uses fork() and is Unix-only), or a working in-process parallel runner (issue #641 reports the parallel-runner example ran every suite on one thread)
Relying on C++20 modules today: issues #713, #697, #650 and #623 (open) report import boost.ut failing, module builds breaking, and tests always skipped when ut is included into a module

integration.min_toolchain: C++20; README lists GCC 9+, Clang 9+, Apple Clang 11+, MSVC 2019+ (asterisked) and Clang-cl 9+ as tested
integration.platforms: any platform with a C++20 compiler; aborts() is limited to Unix-like systems because it uses fork()
integration.thread_safety: not documented; ut.hpp contains no mutex or atomic, so concurrent expect() calls from several threads are not synchronized by the framework

gotchas: expect(a == b) on plain built-in values only prints [false] on failure; to see the operands you must use the UT literals (1_i == 2), that % a == b, or eq()/neq(), which also reject mixed-type comparisons
Test registration relies on static objects and the cfg variable template; across several translation units with some compilers this has produced crashes or skipped tests (issue #637)
With using namespace boost::ut, the framework's nothrow can clash with the libstdc++ declaration (issue #648); throws()/nothrow() exist only when exceptions are enabled (__cpp_exceptions)

The benchmark's 'suite' workloads gave Catch2 and doctest one TEST_CASE with 100 SECTION/SUBCASE blocks per file but gave UT and GoogleTest 100 separate tests, so the execution-time bars for Catch2 (about 1.8 s) and doctest (about 0.5 s) partly measure section re-entry rather than framework overhead
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Against doctest, pick UT for C++20-only code with many small tests per file or when you want macro-free syntax; the 2019 chart shows UT clearly ahead on include-only and single-file workloads, while doctest ties or wins on large multi-file suites and also supports C++11. The cache and distribution siblings (ccache, sccache, distcc, FASTBuild and others) are complementary: they reduce rebuild cost for any test framework rather than the cost of compiling test code itself.
verified_claims_summary: UT's own linked benchmark (cpp-testing/ut-benchmark, 2019) compiled generated test programs one translation unit at a time with clang 9 (gcc 9.2 libstdc++) and gcc 9 in default, -g and -O3 -DNDEBUG modes, timing each cell once with GNU time on an unstated machine: UT 1.1.0 against GoogleTest 1.10.0 and Boost.Test 1.71.0 (prebuilt static libraries), Catch2 2.10.2 (CATCH_CONFIG_FAST_COMPILE) and doctest 2.3.5 (DOCTEST_CONFIG_SUPER_FAST_ASSERTS). Read off bar charts, include-only took about 0.4 s for UT against 0.8-1.0 s for GoogleTest/Boost.Test and 1.3-16 s for doctest and Catch2 (which compile their whole runner in that file), and the 100-file STL suite took about 55 s against 50-195 s with clang9 default.
status_note: Actively maintained (commits through 2026-10-24, latest tag v2.3.1 from 2025-04-02), BSL-1.0 and a single header that is easy to vendor, but the speed evidence is a first-party 2019 run of UT 1.1.0 that has never been refreshed.
